feedback: Written before this candidate has raced. Iteration 0 (±0.02 m spread, 12 mm footprint) gave 100% off-track failure with 1 line-loss event per trial and max_error about 0.061 m, just past the 0.06 m floor on the off-track limit. This supports your reading that the spread is too narrow to recover before the limit. To keep the spread test clean, I did not change the controller gains; I scaled the weights to x/0.02 so steering gain matches iteration 0. Next-race rules: (a) if line_loss_events drop to zero on the s-bend and slalom but max_error still reaches about 0.06 m, the limit is steering response, not visibility, so next raise kp (for example to 3.0) before changing geometry again; (b) if line_loss_events remain above zero at ±0.03 m, the footprint or spread is still too narrow, so move to sensor_size 0.016 m or add sensors at ±0.04 m; (c) if the robot completes with high steering_oscillation on the slalom, the forward lead is the next lever, so reduce y to 0.03 m. Iteration 0 showed progress of only 0.04 on the s-bend, so the speed question stays open until a run completes.
requested_changes: Keep the ±0.03 m spread with 5 sensors and a 12 mm footprint (this iteration) and check whether line_loss_events fall to zero on the s-bend and slalom. Iteration 0 showed 1 loss per trial on all tracks at ±0.02 m, so any remaining loss confirms the spread is still too narrow.

If line loss persists at ±0.03 m, test sensor_size 0.016 m (same positions) to extend tape visibility by about 2 mm per side before adding sensors. Iteration 0 reached the off-track limit at 0.061 m, so a larger footprint is cheaper than a wider spread.

If the robot completes but steering_oscillation is high on the slalom, test forward lead y = 0.03 m (from 0.05 m), keeping the spread fixed, to isolate the lead effect. Do not change the lead before the spread result is known.
